newsitem.title: MEXICO: FOCUS - Mexico moves to halt U.S. sorghum imports.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Mexico moves to halt U.S. sorghum imports.

text.p: Mexico, slyly moving to protect national sorghum stocks, has stopped processing phytosanitary permits to import the grain from the United States, effectively putting in place a temporary import ban.
Grains sources said Friday the move intends to halt imports until nationally produced sorghum inventories, estimated to be around 2.0 million tonnes from the 1996 harvest, are used up.
"They are receiving the permits but they are not processing and expediting them, it is a form of temporarily banning imports," one grains trader told Reuters, requesting anonymity.
Sorghum importers and exporters need no license or quota to bring the grain into Mexico, just a phytosanitary permit from the Department of Food Hygiene, a branch of the Agriculture Ministry.
The move was not announced by the government and is unlikely to be confirmed because of its informal nature, sources said.
But it is causing headaches for U.S. exporters and Mexican importers, especially at the usual Nuevo Laredo U.S. port of entry, because of the suddeness of the move.
Ricardo Celma, director general of Mexico office of the U.S. Feed Grains Council, confirmed the permit denial stance.
"It is a socio-political problem because there is an abundance of grains in the country and everyone's inventories are swollen," he said.

"They should announce what they are going to do, like this, it only causes problems," he said, adding he had received requests for help from mechandisers who faced had shipments lined up and were unable to import them. He declined to name the companies involved.
Celma said the council plans to protest the stance with the Mexican government via Norval Francis, the minister counsellor for agricultural affairs at the U.S. Embassy in Mexico.

"It is logical that first national grains are sold before imports are allowed. We have around 2.0 million tonnes (to dispose of at the moment) there is no sense in importing more or planting more until these stocks are sold," he added.
Sorghum stock problems have been brewing in Mexico for the past two months.
The government was forced to buy up 400,000 tonnes of unsold sorghum from the Tamaulipas crop with farmers there facing bankrupcy because they were unable to sell off stocks at profitable prices.
"This situation could last for months," Celma said, pointing to high sorghum inventories and the solid crops reported in the country's top two producer states Tamaulipas and Guanajuato.

Urbano Ortiz Carranza, president of the National Association of Sorghum Growers, declined to acknowledged the permit processing stance was a deliberate move on the part of the government to halt imports.
In a telephone interview with Reuters, he said, however, there was logic in the government putting up barriers to prevent more imports while internal sorghum stocks were so high.
Also, sorghum growers from Guanajuato started blocking roads in the central state for the same reasons. The government again was forced into action.

The Agriculture Ministry set up a 45-million-peso purse to relieve farmers of interest payments on loans for three months, covering some 500,000 tonnes of sorghum. The government also offered them an additional 40 pesos per tonne on grain sold to offset lower prices.
